newsitem.title: USA: House Republican leaders say tobacco needs study.
newsitem.headline: House Republican leaders say tobacco needs study.

text.p: House Republican leaders made clear Tuesday that Congress would have to study the proposed tobacco settlement for months and possibly into next year.
"That tobacco deal will have to be studied for a long time," House Majority Leader Richard Armey, a Texas Republican, told reporters. "Whether it's next year or not, I don't know the answer."

House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, said he has urged members of Congress to await the outcome of a White House review of the $368.5 billion settlement reached last week by the tobacco companies and 40 state attorneys general. That review is expected to take at least a month.

Under the settlement, cigarette makers would pay $368.5 billion over 25 years to compensate states and smokers and to fund programmes to help people quit smoking. They also would be more heavily regulated. The deal would need legislation passed in Congress to be enacted.

In the Senate, the Judiciary Committee plans on Thursday told hold a hearing to get an overview of the agreement. But no legislation is pending and committee staff said the aim is to make the senators familiar with the proposal.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, has said the Senate could not take up tobacco for at least a few months.

Public health experts, convened by former U.S. Surgeon General Dr. C. Everett Koop and former Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Dr. David Kessler, gather in Washington to review the proposal on Wednesday. Koop and Kessler have already criticised it, saying it would water down the FDA's authority to regulate nicotine.
Armey said he had not yet read the proposed settlement and had no initial reactions as to where changes were needed.

"I'd have to have a staff of experts around," he said, adding that at least three and possibly more House committees would be involved in any effort to pass legislation to enact the agreement. Hearings and debate in those committees will "take some time," he said.
Separately, the parent of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., the nation's second-largest cigarette maker, said it expected its initial payment under the settlement accord to be $600 million.

RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. also said in a filing with regulators that the agreement could have a "significant negative effect" on its tobacco business. But it added that the settlement offers "a measure of relief from certain litigation" that could have seriously hurt its operations.

Meanwhile, both the House and Senate are set to vote on tax cut bills this week. The Senate version includes a 20-cent increase in cigarette taxes that would be used to expand health insurance coverage of children. The House version does not have such a provision.
